To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) parental control and support are associated with less drinking, (2) parental monitoring is associated with less drinking among adolescents, (3) parental support and parental control are associated with less alcohol-related problems, (4) parental monitoring is not associated with alcohol-related problems, and (5) the association between parenting styles and adolescent alcohol use and problems are mediated by self-regulatory factors.

(a) the relationship between parental monitoring and alcohol use is mediated by perceived parental disapproval and (b) the relationship between perceived parental disapproval of drinking and alcohol use is partially mediated by self-regulatory efficacy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social and cultural factors which influence the development of children and the way in which children are brought up.
the development and testing of a social learning theory model of alcohol use and related outcomes in young people.
the social and psychological factors that may influence alcohol use and problems among college students.

the most effective way of reducing underage alcohol use would be through a combination of measures, which include a combination of both supply reduction and demand reduction measures.

the social learning theory of Bandura and Walters (1963) is the most influential theory of child rearing and socialization in the field of developmental and educational psychology and has been the most influential theory for the past 40 years (Bandura and Walters, 1963; Bandura, 1977, 1986; 1989, 2001).

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social learning perspective has been useful in understanding parenting styles and the development of self-regulation, and the relationship of these to alcohol use and problems.
social learning theory is a theory of learning and development that explains how people actively shape and are shaped by their environment.

we have shown that the social learning perspective provides a useful model for understanding alcohol use, abuse, and dependence, and that this model can be applied to the development of interventions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social learning is a powerful tool to improve the lives of children and young people.
we need to think about how the social environment can support the social learning of self-regulation and self-management skills, and how these skills can be used to reduce alcohol use.
parents can play a key role in reducing underage drinking by having conversations about alcohol and by setting rules for their children.
